coreTruths.title: Most dental pain is inflammatory, so first-line analgesia is an NSAID, not an opioid
coreTruths.broaderContext: Dental pain is overwhelmingly inflammatory in origin. That single fact decides which drug works, why opioids underperform, and why prescribing the right NSAID matters more than reaching for codeine.
coreTruths.body:
## Match the analgesic to the mechanism

Most dental pain is inflammatory, so the drugs that work best are the ones with an anti-inflammatory action [1]. Aspirin, ibuprofen, and the other NSAIDs are first-line. Paracetamol matches aspirin for analgesic effect but has no anti-inflammatory action, so it sits as a bridge for patients who cannot tolerate NSAIDs [2].

## Opioids are the wrong tool for ordinary dental pain

Opioids alter pain perception centrally and have no anti-inflammatory effect [3]. There are very few indications for opioids in general dental practice, and dihydrocodeine is statistically inferior to ibuprofen 400mg for post-operative pain [4]. Adding codeine to a simple analgesic has never been clearly proven to help [5].

## NSAID cautions are real but narrower than they look

Ask about aspirin allergy in asthmatics, and avoid aspirin in bleeding diathesis, GI ulceration, or concurrent anticoagulants [6]. NSAIDs may exacerbate asthma and asthmatics carry a higher rate of NSAID allergy, but the Committee on Safety of Medicines does not treat asthma alone as a contraindication. Frank allergy or proven asthma exacerbation does [7].

## Chronic and post-op pain need scheduled dosing

For ongoing or post-operative pain, regular dosing within the drug's half-life beats as-required dosing [8]. Patients who chase pain rather than stay ahead of it use more analgesic and get less relief.

citations.quote: Most dental pain is inflammatory in origin and hence is most responsive to drugs with an anti-inflammatory component, e.g. aspirin and the NSAIDs.

Similar in analgesic efficacy to aspirin but has no anti-inflammatory action and is a moderate antipyretic. Does not cause gastric irritation or interfere with bleeding times. Overdosage can lead to liver failure. Dose: 1000mg 6-hourly PO (maximum dose 4g/24h in adults).
The opioids act centrally to alter the perception of pain, but have no anti-inflammatory properties.

There are very few indications for the use of opioid analgesics in general dental practice. Although dihydrocodeine remains in the DPF, it is statistically inferior to ibuprofen 400mg in post-operative pain relief.

The addition of codeine to the minor analgesics, while never being proven to be of advantage, may have marginal benefits in some cases. No combination analgesics are currently prescribable on the DPF.
Avoid in bleeding diathesis, gastrointestinal ulceration, and concurrent anticoagulant therapy. Ask about aspirin allergy, particularly in asthmatics.

NB: while all NSAIDs may exacerbate asthma and there is a higher incidence of NSAID allergy in asthmatics, the Committee on Safety of Medicines recognizes that this does not constitute a C/I for the use of these valuable analgesics. Frank allergy to NSAIDs or proven exacerbation of asthma is a C/I.
Chronic and post-operative pain require regular, not as-required, analgesia, given in adequate amounts and within the therapeutic half-life of the drug.

coreTruths.title: Antibiotics do not replace drainage, and prescribing follows patient + organism + drug
coreTruths.broaderContext: Antibiotics are an adjunct, not a fix, for dental infection. The reasoning behind every prescription is the same triad: who is the patient, what is the bug, and which drug fits both.
coreTruths.body:
## Three questions before any antibiotic prescription

Good prescribing comes from three questions: who is the patient, what is the likely organism, and what is the best drug. The right choice is safe in that patient, specific to the organism, and deliverable in a reliable form [1].

## Drainage of pus is the treatment, not the antibiotic

Antibiotics do not replace the drainage of pus in abscesses [2]. The drug supports the body once the source is dealt with. Skipping drainage and reaching for amoxicillin alone is treating the wrong problem.

## Know the common bugs and their sensitivities

Most dental infections are treated blind because culture is rarely feasible in practice. That makes it essential to know the common organisms in the field and their sensitivities, and to understand mode of action, absorption, side effects, resistance patterns, and interactions of the drugs being used [3]. Prophylaxis is a separate question with its own logic [4].

## Patient factors change the answer

Allergy, hepatic or renal impairment, immunocompromise, pregnancy, breastfeeding, the oral contraceptive, and age all narrow the field [5]. Penicillin allergy means all penicillins are out, and roughly one in ten of those patients will react to cephalosporins as well [6]. Amoxicillin can interfere with the oral contraceptive and tetracyclines are particularly likely to render it ineffective [7].

## Metronidazole is anaerobicidal, not a generic anti-infective

Metronidazole only covers anaerobes. Useful in NUG and many acute oral infections, useless against aerobes, and severe nausea or vomiting follows if the patient drinks alcohol on it [8]. Pairing it with a beta-lactam covers both halves of a mixed dental infection.

## Resistance has narrowed the toolkit

Tetracycline resistance has grown, and clindamycin has replaced erythromycin for single-dose endocarditis prophylaxis when prophylaxis is indicated [9]. Co-amoxiclav widens amoxicillin's range to cover the commonest cause of head and neck resistance by neutralising beta-lactamase [10].

citations.quote: When prescribing, consider (i) the patient, (ii) the likely organisms, and (iii) the best drug.
Remember prophylaxis (…… Principles of antibiotic prophylaxis, p. 586) differs from Rx with antibiotics, and antibiotics do not replace the drainage of pus in abscesses.

In reality, most infections are treated blind, therefore it is essential to know the common infecting organisms in your field, and their sensitivities. You also need to know the drugs’ modes of action, absorption, unwanted effects, development of resistance, interactions, and techniques available for delivery.
The best drug is the one which is safe in that patient, specific to the infecting organism, and can be given in a reliable convenient form.

Patients influence choice, in that they may be allergic to various drugs, have hepatic or renal impairment, be immunocompromised, be unable to swallow, be pregnant or breastfeeding, or taking an oral contraceptive; consider also the age and severity of the infection.
Patients allergic to one penicillin will be allergic to all; theoretically 10% will be allergic to cephalosporins as well. A history of atopy (e.g. asthma) ↑ risk.
It is also particularly likely to render the oral contraceptive ineffective.

An anaerobicidal drug, and as such effective in many acute dental and oral infections. Classical dose for NUG is 200mg tds PO for 3 days. For other anaerobic infections is more often used as 400mg bd/tds (depending on severity) PO. Available as tablets, IV infusion, or suppository. Main problem is severe nausea and vomiting if taken in conjunction with alcohol (disulfiram reaction). Remember, it is not effective against aerobic bacteria.
Has replaced erythromycin for single-dose prophylaxis of infective endocarditis (…… Principles of antibiotic prophylaxis, p. 586) when indicated.

Co-amoxiclav is amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid. The latter destroys beta-lactamase (penicillinase) and hence widens the range of amoxicillin to include the commonest cause of resistance in infections of the head and neck.

coreTruths.title: Anti-resorptive drugs bind bone for years, so MRONJ is prevented, not treated
coreTruths.broaderContext: Bisphosphonates and denosumab block osteoclast turnover. Their effect lasts long after the last dose, which is why dental fitness has to be sorted before therapy starts.
coreTruths.body:
## The drugs persist long after the last dose

Bisphosphonates bind hydroxyapatite and act on osteoclasts to slow bone turnover. The effect can last up to ten years [1]. That is why MRONJ risk does not vanish when the patient stops the tablet.

## Risk tracks potency and route

Non-nitrogen oral preparations are the least potent. Nitrogen-containing IV preparations are the most potent. Osteoporosis tends to use the milder drugs, while hypercalcaemia of malignancy and bone metastases use the strongest [2]. Incidence of osteonecrosis is probably under 1% in patients on low-potency oral drugs for osteoporosis, but climbs to around 30% in myeloma survivors at ten years who have had extractions on highly potent drugs [3].

## Denosumab and angiogenesis blockers do the same thing under a different name

Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody that suppresses osteoclast formation, function, and survival. It is roughly a million times more potent than etidronate and IV only. Denosumab plus anti-angiogenic agents like bevacizumab, sunitinib, and aflibercept all sit under the same MRONJ umbrella [4].

## Prevention is the only real strategy

There is no established effective treatment for MRONJ once it appears [5]. Get the mouth dentally fit before the drugs start, with the goal that the patient is highly unlikely ever to need an extraction in future [6]. This is a deliberate shift away from the benefit-of-the-doubt approach most dentists are trained in, and the closest analogue is osteoradionecrosis prevention.

citations.quote: These are a range of drugs which act on osteoclasts and reduce the rate of bone turnover. They bind to hydroxyapatite and their effect is therefore extremely long term (possibly up to 10yrs).

They come in differing degrees of potency, non-nitrogen-containing oral preparations being the least potent and nitrogen-containing IV preparations being the most potent. Osteoporosis tends to be managed with less potent drugs and hypercalcaemia and bone metastases with the most.

The incidence is variable but is probably much less than 1% for patients treated with low-potency drugs for osteoporosis, up to 30% for myeloma survivors at 10yrs who have received highly potent drugs and who have had extractions.

Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody that inhibits osteoclast formation, function, and survival. It is used in the treatment of osteoporosis, bone metastasis, and a number of other conditions that result in ↑ bone turnover. It is only available in IV form and is considered a million times more potent than etidronate. Denosumab and other non-bisphosphonate drugs such as anti-angiogenic drugs bevacizumab, sunitinib, and aflibercept still have the potential to cause bone necrosis. This is known as ‘medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw’ or ‘MRONJ’.
The condition appears to be progressive and there is no established effective treatment although several are being investigated.

Prevention is the most useful management strategy and all patients prior to starting bisphosphonates should have optimum dental health established such that it is highly unlikely they will ever need to have a tooth removed in the future. This is a shift away from the ‘benefit of the doubt’ approach most dentists are currently trained in.

coreTruths.title: Anticoagulants and antiplatelets stay on; local haemostasis does the work
coreTruths.broaderContext: Stopping warfarin or an antiplatelet to extract a tooth swaps a small bleeding risk for a real thrombotic one. Modern practice keeps the drug going and controls bleeding locally.
coreTruths.body:
## Warfarin patients with INR under 4 can have routine extractions

Many regions extract as normal in warfarin patients with an INR below 4, with the INR ideally checked within 24 hours of the procedure [1]. Above 4, refer back to the anticoagulant clinic or physician. Multiple extractions or significant comorbidities push the case into a setting that can offer higher-level care [2].

## Stage the work and rely on local measures

Start with a single extraction and add more later if recovery is uneventful [3]. Local haemostatic measures such as packing with oxidized cellulose, suturing the gingivae, and local pressure are the actual mechanism by which bleeding is controlled [4]. Treat early in the day and early in the week so any prolonged bleed has working hours behind it [5].

## NOACs do not need INR but still need local control

Dabigatran (a direct thrombin inhibitor), apixaban, and rivaroxaban (factor Xa inhibitors) do not normally need monitoring or a pre-treatment INR. Local measures are still mandatory [6]. For a higher-bleeding-risk procedure, the patient may be advised to miss apixaban or dabigatran or delay rivaroxaban that morning [7].

## Antiplatelets generally stay running

For clopidogrel and the newer antiplatelets prasugrel and ticagrelor, treatment should be completed without interrupting the medication. Local guidelines come first, and the GMP or specialist gets the call when in doubt [8].

## Atraumatic technique is part of the haemostasis plan

The SDCEP precautions tie it all together: GMP consultation, delay non-urgent invasive work if a course is time-limited, stage the treatment, treat early, atraumatic technique, local measures, and verbal plus written post-op advice with emergency contacts [9].

citations.quote: Many regions’ oral and maxillofacial surgery routine practice is to perform extractions as normal for patients on warfarin with an INR <4. The INR should ideally be checked within 24h of the procedure starting.

Patients with an INR >4 should be referred to their anticoagulant clinic or physician. Patients requiring multiple extractions or with other significant co-morbidities should be seen in an area which can provide a higher level of care.
If multiple extractions are required, a single extraction should be carried out first. Subsequent extractions of two or three teeth at any time may be carried out if recovery is uneventful.
Local haemostatic measures should be taken to achieve haemostasis following extractions, such as packing the socket with oxidized cellulose and suturing gingivae with local pressure.
Treat early in the day and week (allowing time for management of prolonged bleeding).

While warfarin is still one of the most widely used anticoagulants, there is now a group of newer oral anticoagulants including dabigatran (direct inhibitor of thrombin, a coagulation factor), apixaban, and rivaroxaban (inhibit factor Xa of the coagulation cascade). Monitoring is not normally required for these newer drugs and an INR pre-treatment is not required. However, as with warfarin, local measures should still be taken to achieve haemostasis.

Patients taking a NOAC undergoing a dental procedure with a higher risk of bleeding complications may be advised to miss (apixaban/dabigatran) or delay (rivaroxaban) their morning dose on the day of treatment.

Two new-generation antiplatelet drugs include prasugrel and ticagrelor, both alternatives to clopidogrel. It is advised that treatment is completed without interrupting antiplatelet medication. Local guidelines should always be consulted and if unsure the patient’s GMP or specialist should be contacted for advice.

coreTruths.title: Benzodiazepines treat the dental visit, not chronic anxiety
coreTruths.broaderContext: Short-term sedation for a procedure is a legitimate use of benzodiazepines. Treating long-running anxiety with the same drugs is where dependence and withdrawal problems start.
coreTruths.body:
## Short-term sedation is the legitimate role

Short-term control of fear and anxiety around dental treatment is an entirely appropriate use of benzodiazepines. Long-term anxiety control is a different problem, full of dependence and withdrawal issues [1]. Keep the indication tight: the visit, the procedure, the night before.

## Diazepam suits oral pre-medication, midazolam suits IV sedation

Diazepam has a long half-life and accumulates with repeated dosing, so it works best as oral pre-med an hour or two before the procedure [2]. Midazolam is water-soluble and roughly twice as potent, which is why it is the IV sedation drug, titrated 2–3.5mg slow IV with 1mg increments to a usual total of 3.5–5mg and a 7.5mg ceiling per course [3].

## All benzodiazepines depress respiration and impair driving

Every benzodiazepine can depress respiration. Patients should be warned not to drive or operate machinery while on the drug [4]. That warning is not optional fine print, it is part of consent for sedation.

## Children get paradoxical reactions

Diazepam can cause paradoxical disinhibition in children and is not advised in patients under 16 [5]. For paediatric sedation other agents like alimemazine or chloral hydrate are used instead [6].

## Flumazenil is the antidote

Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines specifically. Doses are reduced in the elderly, and it is avoided in children [7]. Knowing it exists is the back-stop for any IV sedation case.

citations.quote: The short-term control of fear and anxiety associated with dental Rx is an entirely appropriate use of the benzodiazepines. It should not be confused with the long-term control of anxiety which is rife with problems of dependence and drug withdrawal.

This has a long half-life and is cumulative on repeated dosing. Like all benzodiazepines, it can cause respiratory depression, therefore patients should be warned not to drive or operate machinery while on this drug. Dose for anxiety/TMD: 2mg tds, maximum 30mg in divided daily doses. Dose for sedation with LA: 5–10mg PO 1–2h before procedure.

This is a water-soluble benzodiazepine of about double the potency of diazepam. Its main use is in IV sedation (…… Midazolam, p. 636). Midazolam may be given in an oromucosal solution form (or the IV preparation) by buccal topical administration. Also popular as a paediatric sedative for suture removal. Dose for sedation: slow IV initially 2–3.5mg 5–10min before procedure at 2mg/min, ↑ in 1mg steps if required. Usually total dose 3.5–5mg. Maximum 7.5mg per course.
Like all benzodiazepines, it can cause respiratory depression, therefore patients should be warned not to drive or operate machinery while on this drug.
Paradoxical disinhibition may occur in children and its use in those <16yrs is not advised.
(Chloral Elixir Paediatric.) 5mL used as a sedative for removing facial sutures. Oral midazolam is an alternative.
A specific benzodiazepine reversal agent (…… Flumazenil, p. 635). Dosages should be ↓ in elderly. Avoid in children.

coreTruths.title: Safe prescribing means modifying for the patient in front of you
coreTruths.broaderContext: Adult doses are a starting point. Liver, kidney, age, pregnancy, and concurrent drugs all bend the curve. The BNF is the first reference, not the last.
coreTruths.body:
## The BNF is the first stop, not the last

The BNF is the definitive prescribing reference, updated every six months in print and monthly online. When unsure about any drug, it is the first line of enquiry [1]. The amalgamated Dental Practitioners' Formulary at the back lists what can be prescribed on FP10 D in NHS dental practice [1].

## Write prescriptions to be read by a tired pharmacist

Avoid abbreviations and write drug names legibly using the generic name where possible. Always state strength and quantity. Use the full word microgram or unit when prescribing those, because abbreviating either is a known source of dosing error [2].

## Doses bend with the patient

Elderly doses are often roughly 50% lower than adult doses [3]. Children differ markedly from adults, with neonatal doses calculated by body weight and older children typically banded as up to 1 year, 1–6 years, and 6–12 years [4]. Severe liver disease usually warrants medical advice before prescribing [5]. In renal impairment doses almost always need reducing and some drugs are contraindicated outright [6]. In pregnancy, avoid where possible [7].

## Polypharmacy and self-prescribed drugs are the trap

Almost any drug can produce adverse reactions, and many are missed. Avoid polypharmacy and never prescribe without a full medical history, including OTC and self-prescribed medication [8]. Suspected adverse reactions go to the MHRA via the Yellow Card scheme; report all serious reactions and any reaction to a black-triangle drug [9].

## Antifungals and antimicrobials interact widely

Miconazole, fluconazole, and related drugs interact with antibacterials, anticoagulants, antidiabetics, antiepileptics, antihistamines, anxiolytics, and several others [10]. Asking about current medication is the line of defence between a routine prescription and a hospital admission.

citations.quote: Extremely useful information is available in the BNF, which is updated every 6 months in print and monthly online. Use this as the first line of enquiry when unsure about any topic concerning drugs. Drugs listed in the DPF (found at the back of the BNF) can be prescribed in the UK within the NHS on form FP10 D (GP14 in Scotland, WP10 D in Wales, HS47 in Northern Ireland).

Avoid abbreviations and write drug names legibly, using the generic name whenever possible. Always describe the strength and quantity to be dispensed. When describing doses, use the units micrograms, milligrams, or millilitres when possible. Do not abbreviate the term microgram or unit (when prescribing insulin) as these are easily misinterpreted.
Doses may need adjustment and are often substantially lower than for adults (often 50% lower).

Children differ markedly from adults in their response to drugs, especially in the neonatal period when all doses should be calculated in relation to body weight. Older children can usually be prescribed for in age ranges, usually up to 1yr, 1–6yrs, and 6–12yrs.
As most drugs rely on hepatic metabolism, it is prudent to seek medical advice before prescribing for patients with severe liver disease.
Doses almost always need to be ↓ and some drugs are C/I completely. Medical advice should be sought.
Avoid if possible.

Almost any drug can produce these, and many are missed. Try to avoid polypharmacy, and never prescribe without being aware of a patient’s full medical history. Always enquire about drugs, including self-prescribed medication.
Report: All serious adverse reactions. Any reactions to ‘black triangled’ drugs in the BNF/DPF.

There are recognized potentially serious interactions between miconazole, fluconazole, and related drugs and antibacterials, anticoagulants, antidiabetics, antiepileptics, antihistamines, anxiolytics, cisapride, ciclosporin, and theophylline. Check what your patient is currently taking.
